generatedProse.concept-context: Psychology placements are hard to assess with a standard exam, because a research lab, a school and a clinical team each ask for different work. So tutors assess what you can show you learned, usually through a reflective account, a portfolio or a report. The grade follows the quality of your evidence, not how busy the placement looked. That makes one distinction decisive: describing what happened earns little, while showing what you learned, tied to a specific moment and to what you would do next, is what gains marks.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two psychology students write up the same placement in a clinical team for assessment.

Tom describes the weeks in order: the sessions observed, the staff met, the assessments watched. It is accurate and complete, and it reads like a diary. But it stays at the level of what happened, so a marker learns what Tom did without learning what Tom took from it.

Amara picks a few moments that taught her something and builds on each. One case discussion showed how the team weighed risk against a client's wishes; Amara explains what that revealed about ethical judgement and how it will change her own practice. Her account is shorter on events but rich in learning.

Both did the same placement. Amara offered evidence of learning, where Tom offered only a record of activity.
generatedProse.summary: A psychology placement is assessed on the learning you can show, not on the activity itself, which is why evidence beats description. You can now explain how the assessment works and why standard criteria are hard, tell evidence apart from description, and prepare strong evidence of your own. With aims set, the experience worked actively, and your learning evidenced, you are ready to make the most of whatever practice your psychology course brings.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's write-up stronger evidence than Tom's?

items.text: She showed what she learned from specific moments and what she would change, rather than listing what happened.
She covered more of the weeks in greater detail.
She wrote more neatly and with fewer errors.
She quoted the supervisor's praise of her placement.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara showed learning from specific moments, and what she would change, which is what makes it evidence.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara showed beyond what happened.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's write-up was stronger evidence because it showed learning from specific moments and what she would change, rather than listing events, polishing the prose or quoting praise.
